title: Safety: Protect People First
subtitle: A home can be cleared, arranged, and spotless and still hold every danger it started with, because tidy and safe are different questions. The fourth S turns from the state of the room to the people in it: look at the home through one new question, could this hurt someone, and fix what could hurt someone worst and soonest, first.

audience: Readers who have finished Chapter 19 and now have a home that is cleared (Sort), arranged (Straighten), and kept clean and read (Shine), three of six S's done, but who sense, correctly, that clean is not the same as safe. Busy home keepers and parents. They do not need to re-argue why we clean or re-run any of the first three S's; they need a way to see the dangers they have walked past for years, decide what to fix first, and handle the worst ones without turning the home into a place of constant dread. A home full of unnoticed hazards is the normal case, because adults habituate to their own space; the fix is a new question and a short triage, not guilt or fear.
core_promise: Turn from the state of the room to the people in it, and make your home safer today without alarm. Learn why a clean, arranged, well-kept home can still be genuinely dangerous (tidy and safe are different questions, and a hazard does not announce itself the way a mess does), and why safety is its own S that comes first in priority. Look at your home through the safety lens, the one new question, could this hurt someone, which the source calls developing safety consciousness. Protect people first: rank the hazards you find by how badly and how soon they could hurt someone, and fix the worst and soonest first, because Heinrich's pyramid means you cannot tell which small danger is the one that will matter, so you remove them while they are still only near misses. Handle the few real dangers plainly, once, so you can stop worrying, and make one first high-value pass on the top dangers today. Safety is love, not fear.
emotional_purpose: Deliver calm, steady reassurance and quiet love, never alarm. This chapter touches real fear (children, falls, fire, poison), so the register is a steady hand: it names dangers plainly, refuses to dramatize them, and frames the whole S as the thing that REDUCES worry rather than stoking it. No shame: a home full of unnoticed hazards is the normal case, because adults habituate to their own space; the fix is a new question and a short triage, not guilt. No fear-mongering, no graphic injury, no alarmist statistics; Heinrich's Principle is used as a reason to act calmly now, not as a threat. The payoff is a parent breathing out, because every hazard removed is a worry you get to set down and never pick up again. Deliver the honest first Safety step: because a part opener that removes real dangers, the needle takes its FIRST Safety step off the Shine-complete milestone, small but honest, because removing the chance of harm is the deepest kind of friction gone. The goal is still ahead, because Safety has only begun and Standardize and Sustain still follow.

worked_example.space: The whole finished home, and the launch pad within it. The home was cleared (Sort), arranged (Straighten), and cleaned end to end and read (Shine, Chapters 16 to 19), and it still holds hazards none of those asked about: a rug at the stair top, cleaning bottles in a low cupboard near a toddler, a dead smoke alarm, a heavy thing on a high shelf, a cord across a walkway, a pan handle turned outward. Chapter 20 sees them through the safety lens, triages them by how badly and how soon they could hurt someone, and fixes the worst today (the alarm battery, the poisons up and latched, the rug at the stairs); even the launch pad gets the new question. Nothing is cleaned or tidied; a few things move, or get latched, or get a fresh battery, purely because they could hurt someone.

Source: the 6S "Principles of 6S: Safety Step" (establish a goal of zero accidents and injuries, identify and eliminate hazards, safety integrated into all other S's, develop safety consciousness, address issues immediately), the 5S+1 history, the hazard definition, and Heinrich's Principle, home-scaled and referenced lightly, tied to Toyota and the Toyota Production System, not overclaimed (especially the precision of Heinrich's ratios).

the_lens_and_triage.the_safety_lens: Change the question. For three parts of the book you looked at your home asking, in various forms, is this in order; now you look at the same home asking something else entirely: could this hurt someone. The rule, frozen: ask not whether it is tidy, but whether it could hurt someone. That single swapped question is the whole tool, because a question decides what you are able to see: ask is this tidy and your eye slides over the dead smoke alarm; ask could this hurt someone and the same alarm lights up. This is what the source calls developing safety consciousness, teaching your eye a new question until asking it becomes automatic. What you are building is not fear; it is a habit of noticing. The hazard definition, frozen: a hazard is any thing or situation in a home that could hurt someone: the loose rug, the pills within reach, the dead smoke alarm, the wobbling shelf. It does not have to look like a mess. Most hazards are perfectly tidy.
the_lens_and_triage.protect_people_first: The triage, because you cannot fix everything at once, and the honest answer to overwhelming is to put the findings in order. The triage, frozen: protect people first, fix what could hurt someone worst and soonest, before anything else. Rank by two plain measures, how badly it could hurt someone and how soon or how likely it is to. A dead smoke alarm and a bottle of pills a small child can open score high on both, so they go to the very top and get fixed today; a slightly loose bannister that holds fine can wait its turn. This is not being casual about the bannister; it is refusing to let it and forty other small things crowd out the two that could actually hurt someone this afternoon. Safety is triage, and triage means the worst first, on purpose, without apology.
the_lens_and_triage.the_pyramid: Why you act on the top of the list now rather than someday, straight from a pattern safety workers have watched for a century. The pyramid, frozen (Heinrich home-scaled): safety work has long noticed a pattern, sometimes called Heinrich's Principle: a large pile of small hazards produces mostly near misses and minor hurts, and, every so often, out of the same pile, one serious injury. You can rarely tell in advance which hazard is the dangerous one. That is exactly why you do not wait for the serious injury to act: you remove the hazards while they are still only near misses, because the whole aim is to never find out which one it was. You are not fixing the smoke alarm because you expect a fire tonight; you are fixing it because the cost of removing a hazard while it is harmless is so low, and the cost of guessing wrong so high, that there is nothing to weigh.

worked_example.applied_pass: Make a start today and keep it small, because protecting people first means the first pass is the worst few things, handled now, not a thorough hunt. Take the lens for a slow walk through the home you know so well you have stopped seeing it. The smoke alarm you cannot remember testing: press the button, and if it is silent, a new battery goes in before anything else on the list, because nothing else you find will matter as much. The cupboard under the sink, tidy and ordinary, full of cleaning bottles at the exact height of a small child: everything that could poison someone goes up high or behind a latch today. The rug at the top of the stairs that has always slid: a strip of grip tape underneath, or the rug gone, because a fall down a staircase is precisely the worst-and-soonest kind of hazard. Even the launch pad gets the new question: is anything heavy stored where it could fall, is a cord strung where a foot could catch it, is there anything at knee height a crawling child could reach. Fix what the lens finds at the top of the list, and leave the rest for the thorough pass that is coming.
worked_example.tally: Notice what the walk was and was not. It was not a deep clean and it was not a tidy; the home was already both, and nothing moved for the sake of order. A few things moved, or got latched, or got a fresh battery, purely because they could hurt someone, and now they cannot. That is Safety in its smallest complete form: one lens, one walk, the worst dangers handled first, not a tidier home but a safer one. Because a part opener that removes real dangers, the friction meter TAKES ITS FIRST Safety step off the Shine-complete milestone toward the goal. This one is honest in a new way: nothing was cleaned or tidied, but the room's exposure to harm dropped, and removing the chance of harm is the deepest kind of friction gone, the near miss that now cannot happen, the worry a parent can set down. The step is deliberately small, because the earlier S's already cleared most of the daily friction the meter measures; what remains (Safety, Standardize, Sustain) protects and locks in, in smaller increments. The goal is still ahead, because Safety has only begun and Standardize and Sustain still follow.
